technique: repetition with a difference — a word or shape returning changed
lesson:
Today we work on one tool: repetition with a difference. That means a word or shape comes back, but changed, so you hear both the sameness and the change.

This poem does it with the word "take." First it says the seed "only takes where the ground's been bared." Then near the end it says "The ground out there will take whatever mark you give it." Same word, but the meaning shifts. The first "take" is about a seed rooting. The second "take" is about the ground accepting anything you do to it.

It works because you hear the word the second time and remember the first. Your mind connects planting a seed to making a mark. The repeat makes you treat your own action like planting.

Try this: pick one plain verb, use it once early, then use it again later about a different thing.

The second time through, wait for "take" to come back and feel the meaning move.

Here is the poem.
poem:
Sauerkraut on the air from last night's crock,
that sour working breath the cold can't quite put down,
and under it the rub gone cold on yesterday's grate,
smoke-ghost of a long cook soaked into the wood.
You wake to the tail of it, the house still holding
its one lit stove, its ember banked for morning.
Out west the full moon's going down behind the ridge,
low and spent, a coin laid flat on the dark—
it climbed when the sun quit, rode the night out whole,
and now the pale comes up to trade it off.
There's seed to go in the cleared strip past the pines,
the fine stuff that only takes where the ground's been bared—

The ground out there will take whatever mark you give it—
go make one that holds.
